title: The kind sacrifice
hook: a king's great sacrifice with no animal killed: gifts to farmers, traders and workers

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sonadanda and his turban, and your line, hand washes hand. Did washing your hands remind you of anything? Today, another brahmin, with a yard full of animals. Day five hundred thirty-four.

Seven hundred bulls. Seven hundred bullocks, seven hundred heifers, seven hundred goats, seven hundred rams. All tied to posts in a village called Khanumata, waiting. The brahmin Kutadanta is preparing a great sacrifice, the kind that was performed for prosperity and blessing in his world. But he wants it done perfectly, and he's heard that the Buddha knows the ancient way of performing a sacrifice, with its three modes and its sixteen requisites. So he goes to ask. Today: the kind sacrifice.
screen: `SEVEN HUNDRED OF EACH, TIED TO POSTS.` → `KUTADANTA WANTS IT DONE RIGHT.` → `HE GOES TO ASK.`

segments.voice: The Buddha answers with a story. Long ago there was a rich king, Mahavijita, who wanted to offer a great sacrifice. He asked his chaplain how. And the chaplain said: first, look at your country. It's full of bandits. Villages are raided, roads aren't safe. If you raise taxes now, you'd be doing wrong. And don't think you can end this with executions and prisons. It won't work. Instead: to those who farm and keep cattle, give seed and feed. To those in trade, give capital. To those who serve the state, give food and fair wages. The king did. And the bandits disappeared, because people were busy with their work. The treasury filled. The text says people played with their children on their laps, and lived with their doors open. Only then came the sacrifice itself. And in it, no bulls were killed, no goats, no chickens, no pigs. No trees were cut for posts. No grass was cut. No servant was made to work by threats or in tears. Whoever wanted to help, helped; whoever didn't, didn't. It was made with ghee, oil, butter, curds, honey and molasses. The Pali word is yañña: sacrifice, offering. The story keeps the word and changes what it means. A sacrifice becomes a gift to the whole country, and then simply giving, and then virtue, and then the path. And Kutadanta? He frees the animals. Seven hundred of each. Let them eat green grass, he says, and drink cool water, and may a cool breeze blow on them.
screen: `A KINGDOM FULL OF BANDITS` · `SEED, CAPITAL AND FAIR WAGES` · `DOORS OPEN, NO ANIMAL KILLED` · `KUTADANTA SETS THEM FREE` · then, large: `THE KIND SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give instead of spend. Think of one thing you were going to buy this week that you don't really need. Hold it in mind. Now picture what that money, or that time, could be as a gift: seed for someone's work, a meal, a fair tip, a donation. Don't decide out of guilt. Just let the picture of the gift sit beside the picture of the purchase. Breathe with both. The bell holds the time.
The kind sacrifice. Yañña, an offering, remade: no blood spilled, gifts to farmers, traders and workers, and the animals set free. Today's word.
Your line: the kind sacrifice. Today, turn one small expense into a gift that helps someone else's work go well. Day five hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions practice dana, generosity, as a central offering: giving food and support to monastics and to people in need, and in many places releasing animals as an act of merit.

fork.setup: you're King Mahavijita's chaplain. the king wants a great sacrifice, but the country is full of bandits. what do you advise first?
options: give seed to farmers, capital to traders and wages to officials.
raise taxes to pay for soldiers.
fork.reveal: the chaplain says force won't end it. support people's work, and the bandits disappear, the treasury fills, and people live with their doors open.

original.note: Pali yañña (Sanskrit yajña): sacrifice, offering. the word kept, its meaning changed in DN 5.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story is just against animal sacrifice.
what it means: it remakes the idea of sacrifice into gifts that let a whole country flourish, then into giving, virtue and the path.

what a scholar hears: the Kutadanta Sutta is often read as early economic advice (support livelihoods rather than punish), and the Buddha says at the end that he himself was the chaplain in that past life.

notes: DN 5 paraphrased. Confirm the numbers of animals (700 each of bulls, bullocks, heifers, goats and rams), the village Khanumata, the chaplain's advice, the 'children on laps, doors open' image, the list of what was not done, the ingredients, and Kutadanta's words on freeing the animals.
The Vedic sacrifice is presented neutrally as part of Kutadanta's world; a Hindu studies reader may wish to check tone.
Confirm that the Buddha identifies himself as the chaplain in the story.
